flashcard_questions.q: What is air pressure in the atmosphere?
flashcard_questions.a: The force exerted by the weight of air above a point, measured in millibars.

flashcard_questions.q: What weather does a low pressure area with rising air bring?
flashcard_questions.a: Cloud and rain, as the rising air cools and condenses.

flashcard_questions.q: What weather does a high pressure area with sinking air bring?
flashcard_questions.a: Clear dry conditions, because the sinking air warms as it descends.

flashcard_questions.q: Which circulation cell lies between the equator and about 30° latitude?
Why are most of the world's hot deserts found near 30° latitude?
flashcard_questions.a: Sinking air at the tropics creates high pressure and dry conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: Which circulation cell covers the latitude of the UK?

flashcard_questions.a: The deflection of moving air caused by the Earth's rotation.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can a tropical storm not form on the equator itself?
flashcard_questions.a: The Coriolis effect is too weak there to spin the air into a storm.

flashcard_questions.q: What are tropical storms called in South-East Asia?
Between which latitudes do tropical storms form?
flashcard_questions.a: Between 5° and 30° north and south of the equator.

flashcard_questions.q: What minimum ocean temperature is needed for a tropical storm to form?
How wide is the eye of a tropical storm?
Which part of a tropical storm is the most destructive?
What wind speed must a storm reach to be classed as a tropical storm?
By how much can a storm surge raise the level of the sea?
flashcard_questions.a: By up to 5 metres or more.

notes: 15 cards: 3 term-to-definition (air pressure, Coriolis effect, storm structure), 3 process-to-effect (low pressure weather, high pressure weather, desert formation at 30°), 2 cell identification cards (Hadley, Ferrel), 2 cause-to-consequence (deserts, no storms on the equator), 5 case-fact cards with a single figure each (latitude band, 26.5°C, eye width, 119 km/h threshold, 5 m surge). The Polar Cell, trade winds, the 60–70 m warm-water depth, the Saffir-Simpson categories, storm season months and the 240–320 km overall width were trimmed to stay within 15.
